notes.1a: (i) A high proportion of candidates knew that copper is metallic. Many candidates omitted that the lattice is giant.
notes.1aii: Diagrams showing the metallic bonding as an array of positive metal ions surrounded by delocalised electrons were varied, with many either omitting or not correctly labelling the positive ions and delocalised electrons.
notes.1b: (i) Some candidates incorrectly referred to a mole of 12C atoms or just an atom of 12C.
notes.1bii: Many correct answers were seen. Some candidates omitted the word ‘average’.
notes.1iii: The full electronic configuration of Cu2+ was frequently incorrect with the 4s2 electrons still present in many answers.
notes.1c: Very few candidates recognised that the ion with an abundance of 23% and an m/e of 31.5 was that of 63Cu2+.
notes.1d: (i) The equation was not well answered overall. Few candidates recognised that it was a redox reaction. Many answers contained electrons on one side of the equation and/or were completely unbalanced.
notes.1dii: The identification of Cu2+ as the oxidising reagent in this reaction was generally not well known. Many candidates answered with just ‘copper’.
notes.2a: (i) Many candidates knew that aluminium objects covered in a layer of aluminium oxide do not react with cold water because the aluminium oxide is insoluble in water and does not react with the water. �PAGE�15
notes.2aii: The equation, with state symbols, was quite well answered, with many candidates recognising that the product was aqueous sodium aluminate.
notes.2iii: It was well recognised that PCl was the required chloride of phosphorus and that HCl is a product of this reaction. Few candidates gave the correct product containing phosphorus. Many answers contained an oxide of phosphorus and/or an incorrect phosphoric acid.
notes.2b: Some candidates gave the formulae of nitrates of elements that are not located in Period 3.
notes.2c: (i) Several candidates correctly stated the oxidation number of Al in AlCl . The answers for that of P in PCl were varied.
notes.2cii: Many candidates knew that Al and P had different numbers of electrons available to use. Many omitted where these electrons are located.
notes.2iv: Some candidates knew the reaction is a hydrolysis reaction with other candidates correctly describing it as a substitution reaction.
notes.3a: Many candidates incorrectly stated, ‘enthalpy change when 1 mole of acid reacted with 1 mole of base’.
notes.3b: (i) Many candidates calculated the initial amount of H SO instead of calculating the amount of acid 2 4 that was neutralised by the NaOH.
notes.3bii: Very few candidates deduced that Q = 5710J and the mass of the solution was often incorrectly given as either 1.00g or a number derived from calculating the masses of NaOH and H SO in the 2 4 reaction.
notes.3cii: Several candidates knew that CH COOH was not fully dissociated, as it is a weak acid, compared to the strong acid HCl, which resulted in a less negative value for the ∆H Very few candidates neut. knew that the difference in values of the respective ∆H values was due to the additional energy neut required to fully dissociate the weak acid such that less energy is released after neutralisation.
notes.4aii: Very few candidates knew that hydrogen iodide is not prepared in the same way as hydrogen chloride because the hydrogen iodide and concentrated H SO would undergo a redox reaction to 2 4 form a variety of products to include SO , H S and I . 2 2 2
notes.4b: (i) A small number of candidates recognised that when a sample of colourless HI(g) is placed in a sealed container and allowed to reach equilibrium the colour changes to purple, attributed to the formation of I (g).
notes.4bii: This question was well answered by many candidates.
notes.4iii: The calculation of the concentration of iodine in an equilibrium mixture was generally not well answered. Candidates who deduced that [HI] is (1.70 ÷ 2 =) 0.85mol in the equilibrium mixture tended to gain some credit. Very few used the expression √(0.0217 × 0.85) to calculate the [I ] as 0.125mol dm–3.
notes.4c: (i) Some candidates were able to describe the difference in composition of the equilibrium mixture at the two temperatures. �PAGE�16
notes.4cii: Some candidates deduced that the reaction is endothermic in the forward direction leading to a lower concentration of H and I in the equilibrium mixture. 2 2
notes.5a: Some candidates deduced the correct empirical formula of C H O from a molecular formula of 3 7 C H O . 6 14 2
notes.5b: (i) Very few candidates used molecular formula, as required in the question, to construct an equation for the reduction reaction.
notes.5bii: Many answers correctly stated that a suitable reducing agent for the reaction is LiAlH .
notes.5d: Many candidates correctly stated that X, the ketoacid, would react with all three reagents to give effervescence, an orange precipitate and yellow precipitate respectively. Fewer candidates recognised that the diol, Y, would only react with the alkaline I (aq) as it contained a CH CH(OH) 2 3 moiety.
notes.6a: The single repeat unit derived from the monomer, CH =CHCN, by addition polymerisation was quite well answered.
notes.6b: (i) Many candidates recognised that the mechanism for step 1 was nucleophilic addition.
notes.6bii: Overall, the mechanism for step 1 was generally not answered well. The polarity on the C=O bond was often absent and the arrow from the CN− to the C (in the C=O bond) did not start from the lone pair on the C of the CN− ion. Several answers contained an incorrect intermediate with a positive charge which was then attacked by the CN− nucleophile and many answers incorrectly showed an arrow from an H+ ion to an O− (in the intermediate).
notes.6iv: The absorptions in the infrared spectrum of CH =CHCN were often correctly identified as CΞN and C=C. Incorrect answers mainly contained an identification of the functional groups rather than the bond or identifying the absorption (annotated as T on the IR spectrum) as that of a C=O group.
notes.6c: (i) Very few candidates gave an accurate description.
notes.6cii: A number of answers were awarded some credit. Few candidates were able to give a full description.
notes.6d: Several candidates gave a correct pair of molecules that were non-superimposable images of CH CH(OH)CN. A common error was diagrams containing the same type of bond at 180° to each other.
notes.6e: The equation for the reduction of propanenitrile to propylamine using hydrogen gas was not well known. Few candidates used the correct stoichiometry for hydrogen.
notes.6f: (i) It was well known that the name of the type of reaction in step 1 is substitution.
notes.6fii: Many candidates gained credit for ammonia. Many omitted heat or the solvent as conditions. �PAGE�17
notes.key_messages:
• Candidates should ensure they know how to correctly complete mechanisms, especially how to use curly
arrows and what they represent.
• It is important that candidates give accurate definitions and descriptions of chemical concepts.
notes.general_comments:
Candidates should be discouraged from using non-standard abbreviations as they do not necessarily
represent standard scientific terminology and are open to interpretation e.g. SE, which may be interpreted as
meaning the shielding effect.
